text: 111. Sir.ḍoḍ. pelo, Bhad., Bhal., Khaś. belo, Rudh. bèla all ‘adze’ — Kal. polát ‘a kind of battle axe’. It is not possible to derive these forms < OIA paraśú- ‘axe’ because of the liquid and because of the voicing of p- to b- in case of the West Pahāṛī forms. This word for ‘axe’ is a wanderwort (see Witzel [2005: 105]), but it cannot have come from Iranian (cf. Cheung [2002: 185f.] for Iranian forms). However, there is a widespread allomorph to this lemma and found in Kal. and Kho., and which indeed is a borrowing from Iranian: taparzíṅ ‘ceremonial axe’ (but Kho. ‘battle-axe’) borrowed from Pers. tabarzīn which is also found in Brah. tafar ‘axe’ and tafarzīn ‘battle-axe’; see also Bng. tɔbri n.f. ‘axe’, S. tabar ‘axe’, Kho.kiv. tap/var ‘axe’ (see also Morgenstierne 1936 [republished 1973: 244]) and Rom. tover ‘axe’. Cheung reconstructs (loc. cit.) Proto-Iranian *tapara- ‘axe, hatchet’ and quotes, among others, Middle Pers. tabrag, New Pers. tabar, Russian topor and Finnish tappara to which I may add Wkh. tʌˈpar ‘axe’, Old Norwegian and Icelandic (norrøn) taparöx ‘axe’. See also Joki (1973: 326). Cheung refers to Gershevitch according to whom *tapara- is < Scythian or Sarmatian *parat- with metathesis.

text: 115. ‘Butterfly’ and ‘flying-fluttering’ (a) Deog. phiphṛi and phimphṛi ‘butterfly’, Kṭg. phímpəṛi ‘butterfly’ (wrongly put in the Addenda and Corrigenda sub pipīlá- ‘ant’ [8201]), Khaśdh. putuṛi ‘butterfly’, Ku. purputaī ‘butterfly’, Jaun. pōtōṭhō, Him. phĩphṛī, Khāśi. phāphṛi, Pāḍ. pāpṛi, Bhal. papṛi, pepri, Khaś. phāphṛi, Bhad. pāpṛi or pepṛõ all ‘butterfly’ — Kurkh. pəpəla ‘butterfly’ — Paṭṭ. phərphitig ‘butterfly’, Chin. pharphiṭig (or phārpitig, Kaul [2006 ii: 42]) ‘butterfly’, Gar. phremolig ‘butterfly’, K. pam pũ̄par ‘butterfly’ (Sachdeva et al. [2010: 60]) — Ind. phirphirì̄ ‘butterfly’, Bur. asqúriṅe phirán ‘butterfly’, Tor.cail. pʌrparʌk ‘moth’, Paš. pheṭiyák ‘butterfly’ — Psht. parkai ‘butterfly’ — Khet. phōpuṭ ‘butterfly’, S. popṭu ‘butterfly’, Jaṭ. popaṭ ‘butterfly, moth’ and bhabbaṭ ‘moth’, Ko.S. phulpã̄khrũ ‘butterfly’ (with second component < OIA pakṣín- ‘bird’), Ko.kaṇ. birbirẽ ‘butterfly’ — Sad. paplā ‘butterfly’ and Kh. pampla, phamphlaʔ which seems (like first word in K. pam pũ̄par) to have Austro-Asiatic parallels: Bahnaric Cua pʌm pil ‘moth, butterfly’, Proto-Vietic *paːmə ‘butterfly’, Sant. pipṛiaṅ ‘butterfly’ and Bon. laʔlaʔp ‘butterfly’, and Mon-Khmer LwAd. poopil ‘butterfly’. Perhaps also related are Kho. pulmuṇḍuk ‘butterfly’, Sh.gur. phōpal ‘butterfly’, Wkh. pilek-miˈlek or pilpilak ‘butterfly’ and Ishk. parparanuk ‘butterfly’, Kamd. prüšpˈulik ‘butterfly; moth’, Bal. pirrik ‘butterfly’. Cf. PIE *pelpel- ‘butterfly’, Latin pāpiliō, Arm. xipilik (loanword?), all ‘butterfly’; cf. also Common Kartvelian *perpel-‘butterfly; wing’, Zan (Laz dialect) parpal-i, Megrelian parpal-ia//parpal-i ‘butterfly; twisting/swirling’; cf. also PTB *pur ‘butterfly’ which, however, is not found in Tib., the only geographically plausible near form is Kann. pʰərpʰitig ‘butterfly’. Generally one can say that many of the above forms got not only ‘indianized’ i.e. they are examples for linguistic naturalization (on this term see p. 223), but also intersected with similar-sounding words e.g. from Austro-Asiatic and Dravidian, and last but not least some of the words may have also been influenced by reflexes of OIA pattrá- ‘wing’ with -ṭṭ- extension (7733) and by the following lemma (b). Cf. also Proto-Dravidian *papla ‘butterfly’ (Pfeiffer [1972: 20f.]) and e.g. Ora. paplā ‘butterfly’, and simimlar “sound-symbolism” forms in Munda (Kuiper [1962: 82]). (b) Bng., Deog. and West Pahāṛī far ‘the sound of a bird’s flight’, Khaśdh. phʌr-phʌr ‘ditto’, Garh. phurr ‘sound of a flying bird’ and pharṛī ‘a banner’, N. pharpharāhaṭ, phyār-phyār, pher-pher all ‘fluttering’ and Khm. phur phur ‘high in the air’, Rab. furut ‘sound of flying away a bird’ (Roy [2011: 100]) — Jaḍ. phur-phurja ‘to fly’ (Z.), Pur. phurcas ‘to fly’ (with infinitive/verbal noun ending), Balt., Nyam-kad and Tib. phur ‘(to) fly’ (other Tibetan forms are phir-, bur-, ur-), New. pharphar, phyār phyār ‘fluttering’ — Brah. firfir and paṛpaṛ ‘flutter; fluttering’ — Ind. phʌ́r ho- ‘to fly’, also in some Sh. dialects puř- and phuri- ‘fly’, Kho. pár ‘sound of bird’s wings flapping’, Bur.ys. pər ɛt- ‘to fly’ — Rj.jaip. bharbhar ‘the noise made by the flying of a bird’ — H. phurr ‘whirring sound (of wings)’ — Sant. phur phur ‘making buzzing, whirring sounds’ (one of Bodding’s examples is with a quail). There is certainly an onomatopoeic component in this lemma and it is unclear to which extend the Tibetan verb was borrowed into surrounding languages. Note also Pers. parper ‘fluttering’, and there are more similar Munda forms: reflexes of Proto-Kherwarian apir ‘to fly’ are found in several modern Munda languages and in Nih. aphir ‘to fly’ (Pinnow [K 501]). Whether or not there is IE influence in this lemma is difficult to say. Influence of OIA *spharati¹ ‘throbs, quivers’ (13820) and of sphuráti¹ ‘spurns, darts’ (13849)  can be excluded because of the different semantic reflexes in Bng. phɔrphɔrāṇɔ ‘to whirl or swirl up (as wind)’ and phurṇɔ ‘to twitch, bat (eye[lash], muscle)’. But it is clear that it is another example of what Mallory and Adams (already quoted above p. 778) describe as an instance “where onomatopoeia has supported their survival.” Cf. also PN *pʰar- ‘to flutter, fly’ (CINCL 101), PAA *par ‘to fly’ (also reflected in PMU **pER) and even Swab. pfurren ‘to flare up with whooshing, buzzing speed’ (von Schmid).

text: 150. The following Bng. lemma has also already been published (Zoller [1989: 189]), but here follows additional data: Bng. mismisaṇɔ ‘to sweat; to drizzle’, mismisɛ n.m.pl. ‘sweat’ and mismisɔ, musmusɔ ‘moist (as earth)’; Deog. mismisɔ ‘damp, moist (as wood or clothes)’, Garh. mosṇu ‘to make wet’ and misauṇyã̄ barkhā ‘lagātār jārī rahne vālī bāriś – long-lasting drizzle’, perhaps also Brah. mīsing ‘to get damp’ and Bal. mis- ‘to damp’ < PIE *meis- (Pokorny and Köbler) ‘to flicker, twinkle; mist’ without RUKI? Cf. German miseln ‘to drizzle’. OIA MEṢ, MIṢ cannot be related here, however note also OIA Dhātup. meṣati ‘sprinkles, moistens, makes wet’. It is also unclear whether also Garh. macmacu ‘turned (a little) wet’ is related here. The origin of this lemma is doubtful.

text: 151. Bng. mundɔ n.m. ‘protection’, e.g., seu tes mundɔ pɔṛɔ (lit: he his protection fell) ‘he was under his protection’. This appears to have an obvious PIE background in *méhar̥ (oblique stem méhan-) ‘hand’, Old English mund ‘hand, protection’ and a corroboration for my earlier published mɔntɔ ‘hand’ (Zoller [1988: 194]). The Bng. word has to be kept separate from Bng. mundrɛṇɔ ‘to close’ as in terɔ śuśu mundru aũ (your breath close.PR.SG.1 I) ‘I strangle you’ which cf. with Brah. mundr ‘constipation’ and both of which are < OIA mudrayati ‘seals’ (10202). Also here close are Him. “mun̆dar” (probably mũdar) ‘the act of prohibiting any impious act at a fair called Bláˈj (Bali-râj)’ with kholṇe (‘to open’) ‘to set free’ but with bándhṇe (‘to bind’) ambiguously not only ‘to order not to do a sinful act at the Bláˈj fair’ but, with same meaning as in Bng., also ‘to offer protection’. This is a meaning not found sub OIA mudrayati ‘seals’ (10202) and mudrá̄- ‘seal, signet-ring’ (10203).

text: 159. Bng. rɔbrɔb n.m. ‘noise, din, racket’, Garh. rabṛāṭ ‘slip of the tongue’ and rabṛāṇ ‘to make a slip of the tongue; to get confused while talking’ — Brah. rabaṛing ‘to babble’ and rabōda ‘chatterbox’. Cf. OIA rebhati ‘creaks (as a car), murmurs (as fluids), chatters, talks aloud, shouts, sings, praises’. According to Mayrhofer (EWA), the basic meaning is ‘sing’ and further IE connections are doubtful, but cf. PIE *reibʰ- ‘to cry, scream, bellow’(?) (IEW: 860).

text: 163. Bng. lɔigɛṇɔ1 v.t. ‘to lick (as animal)’ (with -ɛ suffix), lɔkṇɔ v.t. ‘to lick with a smack- ing sound (children, dogs)’ and likotṇɔ1 v.t. ‘to lick’ (with the ending -ot- perhaps coming from the past participle word liktɔ which only some but not all language con- sultants say to mean ‘moist, watery; licked off’) and lekṇɔ1 ‘to lick’ — Ḍog. lʌkːənā ‘to lick’, P. lakan ‘to lick’, Mult. (a) lakan to lick’ and (b) lakk ‘to lap (as a dog)’, S. lakṇu ‘to lap’, P. lakkṇā ‘to make a lapping sound (as a dog in drinking)’, Brah. lakking ‘to lap like a dog’, Bal. ləkk- and Srk. lək- all ‘to lap like a dog’ — Koh. likōnu ‘to lick’, Sh.gur. likyōnu ‘to lick’ and Sh.dras. lik thyó̄no ‘to lick’, Klm. lēk LH ‘sip’, Dara. likɛnt ‘to lick’, Paš. lag- ‘to lick’ and lak- ‘lecken’, Sh.gil. “likeôki” and Sh.ast. “likeóno” ‘licking’ (Leitner), Sh.koh. līkōnȗ and Sh.gur. likyōnȗ both ‘to lick’ (T. Gra- hame Bailey), Kho. and Kho.kiv. ligini ‘tongue’ — Bun. lak- to lick’. These words appear to be partly same as and partly different from the derivations < OIA *lakk- ‘sound of lapping or bubbling’ (10876). Words with meaning ‘lapping’ are found geographically to the south of the northwest languages which have the meaning ‘lick’. In this western group the meaning has a clear onomatopoeic dimension (‘sound of lapping’) which I cannot see in the northwestern group which is also morphologically more differentiated than the western group which derives in a straight line from the reconstructed lemma. Thus I propose a different origin for the northwestern words with subsequent contamination: (a) Mallory and Adams provide three PIE words for ‘lick’: *leiǵh-, WC-PIE *lak- and WC-PIE *lab-. On *lab- see p. 64. However, there is Munda Sant. lakar lakar ‘to protrude the tongue with thirst, as a. dog; to be faint with thirst’ and there is PTB *m/s/g-lyak ‘lick; tongue’. (b) Note also Common Kartvelian *loḳ- ‘licking’ with many modern reflexes (Chukhua [2019: 263]) and . (c) Ind. lac̣ʌ́ṽ and laṣʌ́ṽ ‘to lick’, Sh. laṣ th- ‘to lick’ and Bur. laṣ -̇t- ‘to lick’ can be derived < older *lak-s- via *lakṣ- as e.g. in Kt. pṣə ‘shaman’ ultimately going back to PIE *speḱ- (‘to see, look’) + *-s. The following Nuristan forms, partly quoted by Turner, namely Kt. lez- ‘to lick’ and Ash. lēs- or lēij̈-, leij- ‘to lick’ and Pr. luzuk(h) ‘tongue’, appear to have developed out of PIE *leiǵʰ- (Strand suggests Pr.Ar. *liǰh-a- ‘licks’) and therefore parallel similar Arm. lezu ‘tongue’ (lizem ‘I lick’) and Iranian *raiz¹ ‘to lick’ but with preservation of the PIE *l. But cf. also Pers. līsīdan ‘to lick’. The bewildering number of the above forms precludes any direct derivations < OIA lihati ‘licks’. Note also PN *lakʰ- ‘to lick, lap up’ (onomatopoeic).
